title: Carbohydrates, protein and fat
summary: Foods often contain several nutrients. Carbohydrate generally has the most immediate influence on post-meal glucose.
why: A bowl of dal contributes both carbohydrate and protein; calling it a protein food alone can miss part of the meal.
how: Starch and sugars supply glucose. Protein and fat influence fullness and can change the timing of the response.
example: A lunch includes chapati, dal, curd and paneer. The learner considers each ingredient and its portion.
caution: Food-group labels are shortcuts. A gravy may include flour, milk or sugar even when its main ingredient is paneer.
question: Does a savoury food contain carbohydrate?
answer: It can. Rice, pulses, flour and milk all contribute.

title: Glycemic index versus glycemic load
summary: Glycemic index (GI) compares glucose responses to equal amounts of available carbohydrate. Load (GL) also accounts for the carbohydrate in the portion.
why: A small portion and a large plate of the same rice share a GI but can have different loads.
how: GL is GI multiplied by available carbohydrate grams in a portion, divided by 100. Grinding, cooking and mixed meals can change the response.
example: A person compares a spoonful of pulao with a full serving rather than ranking the rice by GI alone.
caution: GI tables cannot predict an individual curve or determine insulin doses.
question: Does a low GI make the amount unimportant?
answer: No. Portion and total carbohydrate still matter.

title: Total carbohydrate versus sugars
summary: Sugars make up one part of the carbohydrate in a food. Starch can contribute substantially even when little sugar is listed.
why: Reading only added sugars can miss much of the carbohydrate in bread, biscuits or breakfast cereal.
how: Compare the carbohydrate and sugar entries using the same reference weight. Sugar is already included in the carbohydrate figure under the relevant label convention.
example: A packet of unsweetened crackers shows little sugar but lists carbohydrate from flour.
caution: Do not add the sugars line to carbohydrate a second time.
question: Does “no added sugar” mean carbohydrate-free?
answer: No. Grains, fruit and milk may still supply carbohydrate.

title: Fibre and digestion
summary: Fibre is the part of plant food that resists digestion in the small intestine.
why: It contributes to bowel health and can affect how a meal is absorbed.
how: Food structure matters. Whole fruit and juice deliver different amounts of fibre and can produce different responses.
example: A learner compares a whole orange with strained juice and checks the portion of each.
caution: Fibre reporting differs across countries. Avoid a universal subtraction rule for insulin decisions.
question: Is the fibre in dal the only reason its curve differs from rice?
answer: No. Protein, preparation, portion and the rest of the meal matter too.

title: High-fat and high-protein meals
summary: A mixed meal can affect glucose over a longer period than its immediate carbohydrate response suggests.
why: Checking only an early reading can miss a later rise.
how: Fat may slow stomach emptying. Digestion and later metabolic effects of protein and fat can spread the glucose response over hours.
example: A learner compares several evenings after paratha and paneer with evenings after a lighter meal.
caution: One curve cannot establish a personal dosing pattern. Discuss repeated delayed rises with your team.
question: Is there a fixed delay for every high-fat meal?
answer: No. Ingredients, portion and the person all influence the timing.

title: Portion estimation
summary: A portion is the amount eaten. A reference serving is the amount a database uses to describe a food.
why: Katoris, ladles, idlis and rotis come in different sizes.
how: Weigh a familiar household serving once and compare it with the reference weight. For recipes, account for the cooked yield.
example: A home cook weighs a ladle of sambar and a serving of khichdi. Water changes their cooked weight without adding carbohydrate.
caution: Do not apply raw rice values gram-for-gram to cooked rice. Rasam, dal and curries vary with the recipe.
question: Does a larger-looking bowl always contain more carbohydrate?
answer: No. The ingredients and actual portion weight both matter.

title: Reading food labels in India
summary: Indian packaged-food labels identify a reference quantity and list nutrients such as carbohydrate, total sugars and added sugars.
why: A packet can contain multiple servings, while the nutrition panel may describe 100 g or 100 mL.
how: Match the stated basis to the amount eaten. Convert a per-100-g figure by multiplying by portion grams and dividing by 100.
example: A shopper compares two namkeen labels on a per-100-g basis, then weighs the handful they plan to eat.
caution: Check whether figures refer to dry mix or prepared food. Sugars and added sugars are not extra quantities to add to total carbohydrate.
question: Is the packet’s front claim enough for carb counting?
answer: Use the nutrition panel and the actual portion.

title: Restaurant and street-food estimates
summary: Restaurant estimates start with the visible starches and a plausible serving size.
why: Batter thickness, fillings, sweet chutney and accompaniments can vary between stalls.
how: Split a meal into components such as dosa, potato filling and sambar. Use a close reference food and acknowledge uncertainty.
example: For chaat, a learner identifies potato, puffed rice, sev and chutney before estimating the portion.
caution: A visually similar home recipe is a guide, not a measured value for the restaurant dish.
question: What if the cook cannot give ingredient weights?
answer: Record a reasonable portion description and keep the estimate visibly approximate.

title: Festival foods and sweets
summary: Festival foods can be counted using ingredients and serving weight, just like everyday dishes.
why: Two pieces of mithai can differ in size and in the balance of flour, milk, nuts, syrup and ghee.
how: A batch recipe and its yield give a more useful starting point than the sweet’s name alone.
example: At a gathering, a family divides a known homemade batch into portions and records the piece actually eaten.
caution: A “sugar-free” sweet can still contain carbohydrate from milk solids or grain.
question: Must a celebration meal be all or nothing?
answer: A dietitian can help fit familiar foods into a practical plan.
takeaways: Use the home recipe if known

title: Food choices during exercise
summary: Food during activity serves different purposes, including planned fuel and fast carbohydrate for a low.
why: A high-fat snack may be poorly suited to a situation that needs fast absorption.
how: Duration, intensity, recent meals and active insulin affect fuel needs. Plan with the team before trying a longer activity.
example: A cyclist packs their agreed low treatment separately from a normal lunch.
caution: Do not use a generic grams-per-hour or insulin adjustment as a personal prescription.
question: Why carry fast carbohydrate on a short session?
answer: Glucose can fall unexpectedly even when planned fuel needs are modest.
takeaways: Separate rescue carbohydrate from ordinary fuel

title: Balanced nutrition and weight
summary: Balanced eating considers adequate energy, variety, fibre, protein and enjoyment alongside glucose.
why: Children need enough nutrition for growth. Adults have different needs depending on health and activity.
how: Meals can combine familiar grains, vegetables, pulses, dairy or other protein foods in suitable portions.
example: A family reviews a regular dosa breakfast with a dietitian and explores adding sambar or other foods they enjoy.
caution: Insulin omission for weight control is dangerous. Seek confidential support if eating or insulin feels difficult.
question: Does good nutrition require special diabetes foods?
answer: Everyday foods can form the basis of an individual plan.

title: Alcohol and delayed lows
summary: Alcohol can increase the risk of low glucose later, including during sleep, in adults who drink.
why: The symptoms of a low can be mistaken for intoxication.
how: The liver processes alcohol and may release less glucose. Carbohydrate in a drink can also cause an earlier rise.
example: An adult discusses a monitoring and companion plan before an evening out.
caution: Unconsciousness needs emergency assistance. Never give food or drink to someone who cannot swallow safely.
question: Can an early high rule out a later low?
answer: No. The drink and the liver’s later response can affect glucose at different times.
